newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian budget savings plan faces Senate reform.
newsitem.headline: Australian budget savings plan faces Senate reform.

text.p: The Australian government's plan to introduce a 15 percent tax rebate on earnings from savings faces an uphill battle through parliament with the opposition and other minor parties earmarking it for closer scrutiny.

While stopping short of saying they would oppose it, the Labor opposition, the Greens minor party and the Australian Democrats seized on the savings plan as the one 1997/98 budget measure they would possibly challenge.
"We will certainly be looking very carefully at the savings scheme and the way it is being set up," Greens senator Dee Margetts told reporters.

In its 1997/98 budget announced on Tuesday evening, the Liberal-National coalition government said it would replace a tax cut promised but never delivered by the former Labor government with its own 15 percent rebate on savings income.
Opposition leader Kim Beazley said the savings rebate did not put enough money back into the pockets of voters and would not significantly boost national savings.
Democrats Leader Cheryl Kernot said her party, which has an influential voting bloc in the upper house Senate, would also closely examine the package.

"To get the full benefit if you decide to save through the bank you need to have about A$60,000 squirreled away in an account and 43 percent of Australians earning below A$35,000 now have no savings at all.
"Where's the incentive here for ordinary Australians to save -- it's too tilted towards high income earners," Kernot told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
Between them, the opposition, Greens, Democrats and either of the two independents can block legislation in the Senate.
